issues.item: Triggers: Relationship Reminders: When people say things like my ex
issues.explanation: The trigger 'When people say things like my ex' is difficult to reconcile with a military trauma profile and the rest of the selected items, which center on combat/injury/hypervigilance cues. It introduces an interpersonal/romantic reminder theme that is otherwise unsupported by the memory, threat, appraisal, and strategy items.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Humiliation: I feel permanently humiliated by what happened
issues.explanation: 'I feel permanently humiliated by what happened' is not impossible after military trauma, but in this profile it sits somewhat apart from the rest of the formulation, which is dominated by injury cues, hypervigilance, fragmentation, outsider beliefs, and self-blame. The combination is not a direct contradiction on its own, but paired with the relationship-reminder trigger it suggests a mismatched interpersonal/shame theme that is insufficiently anchored elsewhere in the profile.

vignette:
Liam Fischer was 28 when he came to treatment, a white American man working as a social media manager for a small retail brand, living with his girlfriend and trying to keep up the appearance of an ordinary civilian life that felt increasingly unreal to him. In the Army, he had been involved in an incident that he still struggled to tell in a straight line. When he tried, it came out in broken sections: the hard metallic noise of aircraft overhead, a rush of movement, someone nearby badly hurt, a glimpse of exposed wounds, then his body's surge of fear with no orderly sequence around it. At times he could say a few facts about what happened, but just as often what came first was not an image at all but the full force of panic and horror, as if his body remembered before his mind did. He would stop mid-sentence and say that the whole thing sounded impossible, "like it happened to someone else," because the memory was so extreme that he found it difficult to believe it had really happened to him.

In the months after leaving the military, Liam found that reminders appeared in ordinary places without warning. A helicopter passing over the city could make his chest tighten before he had consciously registered the sound. If he was driving and had passengers in the car, his hands would clamp on the wheel and his shoulders would lock; being responsible for other people in a moving vehicle made him feel abruptly unsafe, as though something terrible could happen again in a split second. The sight of visible injuries on other people could undo him just as quickly. A cut on a coworker's hand, a bicyclist with road rash, even a bloody knee on the sidewalk could bring on a strong physical reaction that felt out of proportion to the moment but impossible to control. He described heat rising through his body, his heart pounding, and a sense that he was no longer fully in the present.

His work put him in frequent contact with images and public settings he had begun organizing his life around. As a social media manager, he spent long hours online, reviewing local event content and community posts. He had started scrolling past anything that showed accidents, injuries, veterans' ceremonies, police photo ops, or people in uniform before he could even think about it. During office commutes or work outings, he preferred to drive alone and became tense if asked to carpool. He knew his avoidance looked rigid from the outside, but to him it felt necessary, a way of keeping himself from being blindsided. He also began rehearsing conversations before almost any interaction, including routine meetings with coworkers and ordinary exchanges with clients. He would plan sentences in advance, trying to prevent himself from freezing, overreacting, or somehow revealing how far removed he felt from everyone else. Over time this made him seem formal and distant at work, and he worried colleagues experienced him as stiff or hard to know.

At home, his girlfriend had noticed that he could not settle at night. Liam often stayed awake long after getting into bed, listening for sounds in the apartment building and feeling that he needed to remain alert. Sleep did not feel like rest; it felt like letting his guard down. If she touched him unexpectedly when he was distracted or half asleep, he reacted with immediate alarm, jerking or spinning toward her before he could catch himself. He felt ashamed afterward, but what frightened him most was how automatic it was. He had also stopped exercising and avoided anything that put his body under strain. Even normal physical exertion felt dangerous to him because the sensations of a racing heart, heavy breathing, and muscle tension resembled the state his body had been in during the trauma.

As civilian life continued, Liam had come to believe that something fundamental in him had shifted permanently. He said he felt like an outsider almost everywhere: in the office where coworkers joked about campaigns and analytics, at dinners with his girlfriend's friends, even with family. He often compared himself harshly to an imagined other person who would have handled things differently and "not gotten into this situation." Alongside that was a settled conviction that he had changed for the worse and would not fully come back. These beliefs were not abstract ideas to him; they shaped how he entered rooms, how much of himself he withheld, and how little future he allowed himself to picture.

He sought help after a recent week in which several things converged. A helicopter had circled low over downtown while he was walking to work, he later saw a man with a heavily bandaged arm in the lobby, and that evening he startled violently when his girlfriend touched his shoulder from behind. The accumulation left him shaken and embarrassed, and he realized how narrow his life had become-how much time he spent scanning, rehearsing, avoiding, and trying to get through the day without being hit by something he could not control. By the time he came in, Liam said he did not know whether he was hoping to feel normal again or simply to stop feeling like a stranger in his own life, but he was clear about what he feared most: that this was the person he was now, permanently damaged and set apart from everyone around him.
